findings.title: Client-side upload validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignores site setting
findings.body: The previous code read the per-type cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it has been replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` (10MB). This is a regression: site administrators who configure `max_image_size_kb` (or `max_attachment_size_kb`) to any value other than 10240 will see inconsistent behavior. Files between the configured limit and 10MB pass the client-side check but are rejected by the server (HTTP 413); files over 10MB are rejected by the client even though the server would accept them when the configured limit is higher. The validation must continue to honor `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`.

findings.title: 413 error message hardcodes 10MB instead of site limit

When an upload is rejected by the server because it exceeds the configured `max_image_size_kb`, the user sees the wrong limit (e.g. "10240 KB") rather than the actual configured limit, which is confusing and undermines the purpose of the setting.

findings.title: Dead duplicate `downsize` method shadows real definition
findings.body: Lines 145-147 define `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149-151 then redefine `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby the second definition wins and the first is unreachable. The live signature is `(from, to, dimensions_string, opts)`, but the leftover four-arg definition is misleading to readers and any caller that still passes `width, height` positionally (matching the dead signature) will silently misbehave because Ruby will treat the fourth positional argument as the `opts` hash. The first definition must be deleted.

findings.title: Animated GIFs cannot be downsized: gifsicle rejects percentage strings
findings.body: The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. For `.gif` inputs with `allow_animation: true`, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated` (lines 137-139), which forwards to `resize_instructions_animated` (lines 115-124). That helper shells out to `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` requires pixel dimensions (`WxH`) and does not accept percentage strings like `"80%"`, so the command fails. `convert_with` swallows the failure (it only logs), the return value is ignored by the controller, the file size never decreases, and after 5 iterations the oversized file is uploaded anyway. The downsize path must either pass pixel dimensions, compute an actual size target from `max_image_size_kb`, or use an ImageMagick-only path for the size-reduction loop (the thumbnail for the post can still be done with gifsicle separately).

findings.title: Loop continues without checking whether downsize succeeded or met the target
findings.body: After the downsize attempt, the controller neither checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize` nor verifies that `tempfile.size` actually shrank. A failure (e.g. animated GIF, broken image, ImageMagick error) leaves the file at its original size, so the `attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` guard is satisfied until `attempt` runs out, at which point `Upload.create_for` is called with an oversized file. The user receives no indication that automatic downsizing failed and the resulting upload will be rejected (or worse, stored over the limit) downstream. After the loop, the code must verify `tempfile.size <= SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and return an error payload (with an i18n message) when it is not.

findings.title: Synchronous ImageMagick downsize runs on the upload request thread
findings.body: The downsize loop runs up to five ImageMagick invocations inline in `create_upload`, which is called from `UploadsController#create` either directly (API synchronous path) or via `Scheduler::Defer` (asynchronous path). For images up to 10MB and concurrent uploads, blocking the worker on CPU-bound image processing for many seconds per upload will back up the queue and lengthen upload latency. The resize work should be moved into a dedicated background job (`Jobs.enqueue(:downsize_upload, ...)` or similar) and the controller should merely mark the upload as `pending_optimization`.

findings.title: URL-downloaded tempfiles are now trusted up to 10MB before validation
findings.body: `FileHelper.download` is called with `10.megabytes` instead of the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. Combined with the new in-process downsize, any user (when `is_api?`) can submit a URL pointing to a 10MB payload, force a full download, and only then attempt downsizing. There is no rate limit, content-type check before download, or guard against repeated large fetches, so this widens the resource-exhaustion surface for the API. The download cap should remain bounded by `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (with a configurable, smaller multiple) rather than a hardcoded 10MB, and/or the URL path should require admin privileges.

findings.title: New automatic-downsize feature has no tests
findings.body: The PR adds non-trivial logic (size reduction loop, animated handling, integration with `OptimizedImage.downsize`, the new dimension-string API, and the change to URL download limits) but the changed-files list contains only production source. There are no controller specs verifying that oversized images are actually reduced, that GIFs in `allow_animation` mode are handled, that failures surface as errors, that the loop terminates, or that URL-downloaded files are bounded correctly. At minimum: a spec that an oversized PNG is downsized and accepted; a spec for an oversized animated GIF; a spec for the case where the image cannot be reduced below the limit within 5 attempts; and a spec for the JS-side validation against the site setting.
